section_title: 2.8. The English Constitutional Heritage: Magna Carta to the English Bill of Rights
note: Section 2.8 is the only section in the corpus that actually defines the rule of law — “even the king is subject to the law, not above it ... no ruler has unlimited authority” — and it traces that principle, plus due process, from Magna Carta and the English Bill of Rights into the U.S. Constitution (Fifth/Fourteenth Amendments, limited government). That matches both the definitional verb and the “influence on the development of legal and governmental systems in the United States” half of the standard.

Section 7.3 Elections is the corpus's section on the election process itself. Its own stated objectives are to describe the stages in the election process, compare the primary and caucus systems, and summarize how primary returns lead to the nomination of party candidates, and its text covers nomination rules, closed/open/top-two primaries, caucuses, campaign-finance law and the FEC as they apply to state, local and presidential contests - the election and voting process at the local, state and national levels that SS.7.CG.2.6 requires.

Section 8.4 is the only section whose own stated objectives are about detecting bias in political communications ("Identify forms of bias that exist in news coverage and ways the media can present biased coverage") and it then works through framing, priming and agenda-setting to show how such coverage shapes public opinion - the second half of this standard's clarifications. Its body text is the substantive teaching on media bias and its effects on what citizens think.

Section 2.3 is the one narrative section in the corpus whose own stated objectives include "Summarize the core features of the structure of U.S. government under the Constitution", and its text states outright that the first three articles divide the national government into three branches and describe the powers and responsibilities of each - exactly the structure-and-function recognition this standard asks for. No other single section covers all three branches: chapters 11, 12 and 13 each treat only one branch.
